reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO nutrition guidance
clinicalPearls: Selenium is an antioxidant trace element, and deficiency is classically linked to Keshan disease, an endemic cardiomyopathy, and Kashin-Beck disease, an osteoarthropathy
It occurs in geographic regions with selenium-poor soil and in patients on long-term unsupplemented parenteral nutrition
Manifestations can include cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy with weakness, and macrocytosis, and long-term deficiency may impair immune and thyroid function
Deficiency in Keshan disease areas is thought to increase susceptibility to a viral cofactor in producing the cardiomyopathy
Serum or plasma selenium and glutathione peroxidase activity help assess status
Repletion can prevent progression of the cardiomyopathy but may not reverse established myocardial damage
It should be considered in patients on prolonged artificial nutrition who develop unexplained cardiac or muscle disease
reference.pathophysiology: Selenium is incorporated into selenoproteins, notably the glutathione peroxidases and thioredoxin reductases that defend cells against oxidative damage, and into the deiodinases that convert thyroxine to active triiodothyronine. Deficiency reduces antioxidant defence, leaving tissues, especially cardiac and skeletal muscle, vulnerable to oxidative injury, which underlies the cardiomyopathy and myopathy. In endemic regions low soil selenium lowers intake across the population, and an interaction with viral infection is implicated in the pathogenesis of the endemic cardiomyopathy. Impaired deiodinase function can also affect thyroid hormone metabolism.
additionalDifferentials: Primary osteoarthropathy for the Kashin-Beck phenotype
Other trace element deficiencies in parenteral nutrition
additionalInvestigations: Erythrocyte glutathione peroxidase activity as a functional marker
Cardiac assessment including echocardiography where cardiomyopathy is suspected
Assessment for coexisting trace element deficiencies in long-term parenteral nutrition
redFlags: Heart failure or arrhythmia from selenium-deficiency cardiomyopathy
Progressive skeletal myopathy with significant weakness
Unexplained cardiac or muscle disease in a patient on long-term parenteral nutrition
Deterioration despite treatment suggesting established irreversible myocardial damage
reference.prognosis: Repletion can halt progression and prevent deficiency-related disease, and early cardiomyopathy may improve, but established myocardial damage in Keshan disease may be irreversible.
pitfalls: Omitting trace element supplementation, including selenium, during long-term parenteral nutrition
Overlooking selenium deficiency as a reversible contributor to cardiomyopathy or myopathy
Failing to consider geographic and dietary risk in endemic regions
Assuming repletion will reverse advanced established cardiac damage
